summary: This RFC reproduces the Host/Host Protocol developed by the ARPA Network Working Group between 1969 and 1971. It managed communication between processes on separate Hosts, covering multiplexing, addressing, flow control, and connection setup. It has historic status.

eli5.summary: Before today's internet, the ARPANET needed rules for computers to talk. This is a copy of those old rules. They are historic now.

subtitle: The protocol that connected computers on the original ARPANET.

tldr.problem: In the late 1960s, the ARPA Network needed a protocol for different computers to exchange messages and coordinate on process-to-process communication, despite having different hardware, operating systems, and word lengths.
tldr.mechanism: The Host/Host Protocol (also called the Network Control Program, or NCP) provided connection establishment, data flow control, and error handling over a simplex (one-way) link model, with support for multiple concurrent connections through sockets and flow control counters.
tldr.outcome: The protocol was the official standard from January 1972 until TCP/IP replaced it in January 1983. Its concepts—sockets, control messages, and connection-oriented communication—influenced the design of TCP/IP.

today: RFC 6529 is Historic. The Host/Host Protocol was replaced by TCP/IP in January 1983 and has not been used in production for over 40 years. However, its design influenced TCP/IP profoundly: the socket concept, the three-way handshake for connection setup, flow control, and the separation of control and data paths all appear in TCP. The document is published here to fill a gap in the historical record—the Host/Host Protocol was standardized before the RFC numbering system was created, leaving it out of the official archives until now.

sections.title: Communication Between Different Computers
sections.content:
The ARPA Network was built in the late 1960s to let geographically separated computers communicate. Each computer (called a Host) was connected through a small specialized computer called an Interface Message Processor (IMP), and the IMPs formed a store-and-forward network. The IMP network handled the hardware details—routing messages, dealing with different link types—but it had a limitation: it only knew about Hosts, not the individual processes running on each Host.

A single Host might be running multiple programs simultaneously, and each program might want to use the network independently. The Host/Host Protocol solved this by introducing a higher layer: it let processes communicate with each other across the network. It also addressed a practical problem: different Hosts had different word lengths (8 bits, 18 bits, 36 bits), so a protocol designed for one would fail on another. The Host/Host Protocol solved this by letting each connection negotiate a connection byte size that both ends could work with.
sections.eli5: The ARPANET had computers with different hardware. The early protocol needed to let programs on different computers talk, even if they had different word sizes, and handle multiple programs on the same computer talking at the same time.

sections.title: Sockets and Connections
sections.content:
The Host/Host Protocol introduced the concept of a socket: a numbered endpoint on a Host that represents one side of a connection. A socket is identified by the Host number and a 32-bit socket number. Each socket has a gender: a send socket (odd) or a receive socket (even). A connection is always between one send socket and one receive socket, so the genders are opposite.

A connection links a send socket on one Host to a receive socket on another (or the same) Host. Once established, a connection carries data in one direction only—it is simplex. If two processes need to talk both ways, they must establish two connections. Connections are set up by exchanging requests for connection (RFCs): an STR (sender-to-receiver) command announces the byte size, and an RTS (receiver-to-sender) command assigns a link number over which data will flow. Once matched RFCs are exchanged, the connection is established.
sections.eli5: Every endpoint for sending or receiving has a number, called a socket. Send and receive sockets connect to each other (one direction each). You set up a connection by each side saying "I want to connect, here are my details," and once they match, data flows.

sections.title: Managing Data Flow
sections.content:
One major concern was that a receiving Host might not be able to handle data as fast as the sender transmits it. The Host/Host Protocol solved this with a flow control mechanism. The receiver allocates buffer space to the sender by sending an ALL (allocate) command, specifying both message space (how many messages can be buffered) and bit space (total bytes of data). The sender tracks two counters (message counter and bit counter) and never sends more data than the receiver has allocated.

If the receiver runs out of space, it can ask the sender to return some of its allocation with a GVB (give-back) command, and the sender responds with an RET (return) command. This negotiated flow control allows receivers to pace senders, preventing buffer overflows. To ensure proper synchronization, the receiver is prohibited from allowing the sender's message counter to exceed 65,535 or the bit counter to exceed 4,294,967,295.
sections.eli5: The receiver tells the sender "I have room for 100 messages and 50,000 bits," and the sender keeps count. If the receiver gets full, it can ask for that space back, and the sender returns it.

sections.title: Opening and Closing Connections
sections.content:
The protocol handles the full lifecycle of a connection through control commands. A connection begins when matching RFCs (STR and RTS) are exchanged. Importantly, an RFC does not have a prescribed lifetime: a Host can queue an incoming RFC indefinitely while waiting for a local process to claim the socket, or it can reject RFCs immediately if it does not have a matching one ready. This flexibility allowed asynchronous connection setup.

Connections end with the CLS (close) command. Both sides must send and receive a CLS before the sockets are free for new connections. The protocol even handles the tricky case where one side initiates closure while the other side is still sending: the sender's CLS means "no more data coming," while the receiver's CLS means "I'm demanding you stop." The document acknowledges that race conditions can occur (for example, if both sides send CLS simultaneously, or if one side sends CLS while the other sends an RFC), but the protocol is designed so these race conditions resolve unambiguously.
sections.eli5: To connect, both sides exchange RFCs. To disconnect, both sides exchange CLS commands. The protocol handles race conditions where both sides try to close at the same time.

sections.title: Message Format and Commands
sections.content:
Every Host-to-Host message has a 72-bit header designed to work with common word lengths (72 is the least common multiple of 8, 18, and 36). The header includes the 32-bit IMP leader (which the IMP network added), a connection byte size, a byte count, and reserved fields. Data follows the header, and then padding fills out to a word boundary.

Control messages are sent over a special control link (link 0) and contain one or more control commands. Each command starts with an 8-bit opcode. Commands include STR and RTS for connection setup, CLS for closure, ALL and GVB for flow control, RET for returning space, INR and INS for interrupts (allowing one side to signal the other), ECO and ERP for testing connectivity (echo request/reply), RST and RRP for resetting connection tables, and ERR for reporting protocol errors. The protocol also includes NOP (no operation) for padding.
sections.eli5: Every message has a 72-bit header with addressing and bookkeeping. Control messages over a special link carry commands like "connect," "disconnect," "allocate buffer space," and "test if you're alive."
